tagline: A forest reservoir and a charcoal kiln mark the journey to Walker.
intro: The Walker Road corridor takes in Lynx Lake in the Bradshaw Mountains and the settlement of Walker. At the lake, ponderosa pine grows alongside beargrass, cliff-rose and alligator juniper.

Yavapai County adopted Walker Road as a Scenic/Historic Route on June 21, 2023. The nearby Walker Charcoal Kiln preserves an older industrial connection: its interpretive sign credits Jake and Joe Carmichael with building it around 1880 to turn oak into fuel for smelters.

Traveling toward Walker, Lynx Lake comes first, six miles below the settlement. The kiln lies near Walker in Prescott National Forest, in the vicinity of the abandoned Poland Junction Mine near Renegade Hill’s summit. The journey ends at the community named for nineteenth-century mountain man Joseph R. Walker.

moments.title: Lynx Lake
moments.text: Lynx Lake began with a dam: Arizona Game and Fish completed the barrier across Lynx Creek in 1963, six miles below Walker. The reservoir sits at 5,530 feet in Prescott National Forest, in the Bradshaw Mountains. Ponderosa pine, alligator juniper, beargrass and cliff-rose grow in the area. Native animals in the area include mule deer, bald eagles, osprey and javelinas. A later mechanical problem changed the lake’s story: in December 2024, Arizona Game and Fish announced plans to drain it because an outlet valve had failed in the open position.

moments.title: Walker Charcoal Kiln
moments.text: The Walker Charcoal Kiln links the forest to the smelters that used charcoal made from its oak. A sign at the kiln credits Jake and Joe Carmichael with its construction around 1880. The same sign explains that charcoal production and mine props required heavy cutting of the surrounding forest in the late nineteenth century. The structure stands near Renegade Hill’s summit, in the vicinity of the abandoned Poland Junction Mine.

moments.title: Walker
moments.text: Walker carries the name of nineteenth-century mountain man Joseph R. Walker. Its population fell from 200 in 1890 to 39 in 1920. The settlement stands at an estimated elevation of 6,289 feet above sea level.
